quotes.text: To the gods I am indebted for having good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good associates, good kinsmen and friends, nearly everything good.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Every moment think steadily as a Roman and a man to do what thou hast in hand with perfect and simple dignity, and feeling of affection, and freedom, and justice, and to give thyself relief from all other thoughts.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: No man will hinder thee from living according to the reason of thy own nature: nothing will happen to thee contrary to the reason of the universal nature.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: To live according to Nature is to live according to a man's whole nature, not according to a part of it, and to reverence the divinity within him as the governor of all his actions.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Pain is either an evil to the body—then let the body say what it thinks of it—or to the soul; but it is in the power of the soul to maintain its own serenity and tranquillity, and not to think that pain is an evil.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Consider thyself to be dead, and to have completed thy life up to the present time; and live according to nature the remainder which is allowed thee.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: To my own free will the free will of my neighbor is just as indifferent as his poor breath and flesh.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Keep thyself then simple, good, pure, serious, free from affectation, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, strenuous in all proper acts.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: To him who is penetrated by true principles even the briefest precept is sufficient, and any common precept, to remind him that he should be free from grief and fear.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: In the constitution of the rational animal I see no virtue which is opposed to justice; but I see a virtue which is opposed to love of pleasure, and that is temperance.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Try how the life of the good man suits thee, the life of him who is satisfied with his portion out of the whole, and satisfied with his own just acts and benevolent disposition.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: The safety of life is this, to examine everything all through, what it is itself, that is its material, what the formal part; with all thy soul to do justice and to say the truth.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: With respect to pain, then, and pleasure, or death and life, or honor and dishonor, which the universal nature employs equally, whoever is not equally affected is manifestly acting impiously.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Dye it then with a continuous series of such thoughts as these: for instance, that where a man can live, there he can also live well.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Do not waste the remainder of thy life in thoughts about others, when thou dost not refer thy thoughts to some object of common utility.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: One thing here is worth a great deal, to pass thy life in truth and justice, with a benevolent disposition even to liars and unjust men.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Always bear this in mind; and another thing too, that very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Do not despise death, but be well content with it, since this too is one of those things which nature wills.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Whatever man thou meetest with, immediately say to thyself: What opinions has this man about good and bad?
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Every man should live in such a way as to discharge his duty, and to trouble himself about nothing else.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: I do my duty: other things trouble me not; for they are either things without life, or things without reason, or things that have rambled and know not the way.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Be not dissatisfied then that thou must live only so many years and not more; for as thou art satisfied with the amount of substance which has been assigned to thee, so be content with the time.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: He who does not know what the world is, does not know where he is.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: Pass then through this little space of time conformably to nature, and end thy journey in content, as an olive falls off when it is ripe, blessing nature who produced it, and thanking the tree on which it grew.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: About pain: the pain which is intolerable carries us off; but that which lasts a long time is tolerable; and the mind maintains its own tranquillity by retiring into itself, and the ruling faculty is not made worse.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius

quotes.text: If a man is unhappy, remember that his unhappiness is his own fault; for God has made all men to be happy, to be free from perturbations.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Be willing at length to be approved by yourself, be willing to appear beautiful to God, desire to be in purity with your own pure self and with God.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Great is the combat, divine is the work; it is for kingship, for freedom, for happiness, for freedom from perturbation.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Practise sometimes a way of living like a person out of health that you may at some time live like a man in health.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Confidence (courage) then ought to be employed against death, and caution against the fear of death.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do you seek a reward for a good man greater than doing what is good and just?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: No one then who is in a state of fear or sorrow or perturbation is free; but whoever is delivered from sorrows and fears and perturbations, he is at the same time also delivered from servitude.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Let death and exile and every other thing which appears dreadful be daily before your eyes; but most of all death: and you will never think of anything mean nor will you desire anything extravagantly.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do not desire to be thought to know anything; and though you should appear to others to be somebody, distrust yourself.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If it be his pleasure that you should enact a poor man, or a cripple, or a ruler, or a private citizen, see that you act it well.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If you encounter a handsome person, you will find continence the faculty needed; if pain, then fortitude; if reviling, then patience.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If you ever happen to turn your attention to externals, for the pleasure of anyone, be assured that you have ruined your scheme of life.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If you would improve, be content to be thought foolish and dull with regard to externals.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: A man’s master is he who is able to confer or remove whatever that man seeks or shuns.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If you wish your children and your wife and your friends to live forever, you are foolish, for you wish things to be in your power which are not so, and what belongs to others to be your own.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Remember, then, that if you attribute freedom to things by nature dependent and take what belongs to others for your own, you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed, you will find fault both with gods and men.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Whoever then would be free, let him wish nothing, let him decline nothing, which depends on others; else he must necessarily be a slave.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Be content, then, in everything, with being a philosopher; and if you wish to seem so likewise to anyone, appear so to yourself, and it will suffice you.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Consider first, man, what the matter is, and what your own nature is able to bear.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Never proclaim yourself a philosopher, nor make much talk among the ignorant about your principles, but show them by actions.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: The condition and characteristic of a vulgar person is that he never looks for either help or harm from himself, but only from externals.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: As in walking you take care not to tread upon a nail, or turn your foot, so likewise take care not to hurt the ruling faculty of your mind.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Begin by prescribing to yourself some character and demeanor, such as you may preserve both alone and in company.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Consider not what he does, but what you are to do to keep your own will in a state conformable to nature, for another cannot hurt you unless you please.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is that he looks to himself for all help or harm.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It is as great a folly to fear death as to fear old age; nay, as to fear life itself; for he that would not die ought not to live, since death is the condition of life.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: The true felicity of life is to be free from perturbations, to understand our duties towards God and man: to enjoy the present without any anxious dependence upon the future.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: We die daily, and while we are growing, our life decreases; every moment that passes takes away part of it; all that is past is lost; nay, we divide with death the very instant that we live.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: A man of business cannot in truth be said to live, and not one of a thousand understands how to do it: for how to live, and how to die, is the lesson of every moment of our lives: all other arts have their masters.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: The present is but a moment, and perpetually in flux; the time past, we call to mind when we please, and it will abide the examination and inspection.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: He that would be truly happy, must think his own lot best, and so live with men, as considering that God sees him, and so speak to God as if men heard him.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: I will live and die with this testimony, that I loved good studies, and a good conscience; that I never invaded another man’s liberty; and that I preserved my own.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: We live as we should never die, and without any thought of human frailty, when yet the very moment we bestow upon this man or thing, may, peradventure, be our last.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: Life is to be measured by action, not by time; a man may die old at thirty, and young at fourscore: nay, the one lives after death, and the other perished before he died.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: A good man is happy within himself, and independent upon fortune: kind to his friend, temperate to his enemy, religiously just, indefatigably laborious; and he discharges all duties with a constancy and congruity of actions.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: It is no great business for a poor man to preach the contempt of riches, or for a rich man to extol the benefits of poverty, because we do not know how either the one or the other would behave himself in the contrary condition.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: It is the bounty of nature that we live; but of philosophy that we live well, which is in truth a greater benefit than life itself.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: It is a blessed thing to dispatch the business of life before we die, and then to expect death in the possession of a happy life.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: Every man has his weak side; let us learn which that is, and take a care of it; for the same thing does not work upon all men alike.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: A plain-dealing sincerity of manners makes a man’s life happy, even in despite of scorn and contempt, which is every clear man’s fate.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: The whole duty of man may be reduced to the two points of abstinence and patience; temperance in prosperity, and courage in adversity.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: He is the happy man that is the master of himself, and triumphs over the fear of death, which has overcome the conquerors of the world.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: No man is born wise; but wisdom and virtue require a tutor, though we can easily learn to be vicious without a master.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: The joy of a wise man stands firm without interruption; in all places, at all times, and in all conditions, his thoughts are cheerful and quiet.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: The truth of it is, there is but one chain that holds all the world in bondage, and that is the love of life.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: He that lives according to reason shall never be poor, and he that governs his life by opinion shall never be rich: for nature is limited, but fancy is boundless.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: A wise man is never so busy as in the solitary contemplation of God and the works of Nature.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: Never pronounce any man happy that depends upon fortune for his happiness; for nothing can be more preposterous than to place the good of a reasonable creature in unreasonable things.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: A good conscience is the testimony of a good life, and the reward of it.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: A wise man, in what condition soever he is will be still happy, for he subjects all things to himself, because he submits himself to reason, and governs his actions by council, not by passion.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: An honest life is not a greater good than an honest death.
quotes.author: Seneca

quotes.text: The superior man does not promote a man simply on account of his words, nor does he put aside good words because of the man.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;— this is knowledge.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: I have seen men die from treading on water and fire, but I have never seen a man die from treading the course of virtue.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The mind of the superior man is conversant with righteousness; the mind of the mean man is conversant with gain.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The determined scholar and the man of virtue will not seek to live at the expense of injuring their virtue.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: Friendship with the upright; friendship with the sincere; and friendship with the man of much observation:— these are advantageous.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The superior man, in the world, does not set his mind either for anything, or against anything; what is right he will follow.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The man of virtue makes the difficulty to be overcome his first business, and success only a subsequent consideration;— this may be called perfect virtue.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The wise are free from perplexities; the virtuous from anxiety; and the bold from fear.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The wise find pleasure in water; the virtuous find pleasure in hills.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The superior man thinks of virtue; the small man thinks of comfort.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: A scholar, whose mind is set on truth, and who is ashamed of bad clothes and bad food, is not fit to be discoursed with.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The superior man may indeed have to endure want, but the mean man, when he is in want, gives way to unbridled license.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: If a man can for one day subdue himself and return to propriety, all under heaven will ascribe perfect virtue to him.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The superior man seeks to perfect the admirable qualities of men, and does not seek to perfect their bad qualities.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The superior man is anxious lest he should not get truth; he is not anxious lest poverty should come upon him.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: Men of principle are sure to be bold, but those who are bold may not always be men of principle.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: I will not be afflicted at men's not knowing me; I will be afflicted that I do not know men.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The superior man is affable, but not adulatory; the mean man is adulatory, but not affable.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: A man can enlarge the principles which he follows; those principles do not enlarge the man.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The progress of the superior man is upwards; the progress of the mean man is downwards.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The superior man is satisfied and composed; the mean man is always full of distress.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: The firm, the enduring, the simple, and the modest are near to virtue.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue.
quotes.author: Confucius

quotes.text: He who devotes himself to learning (seeks) from day to day to increase (his knowledge); he who devotes himself to the Tao (seeks) from day to day to diminish (his doing).
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: To those who are good (to me), I am good; and to those who are not good (to me), I am also good;—and thus (all) get to be good.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: To know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment); not to know (and yet think) we do know is a disease.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong. (So it is with) all things.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: The reason why heaven and earth are able to endure and continue thus long is because they do not live of, or for, themselves.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: My words are very easy to know, and very easy to practise; but there is no one in the world who is able to know and able to practise them.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: Keep life and lose those other things; Keep them and lose your life:—which brings Sorrow and pain more near?
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: In the Way of Heaven, there is no partiality of love; it is always on the side of the good man.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: Men resort to him, and receive no hurt, but (find) rest, peace, and the feeling of ease.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: He who lightly promises is sure to keep but little faith; he who is continually thinking things easy is sure to find them difficult.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: The perception of what is small is (the secret of) clear-sightedness; the guarding of what is soft and tender is (the secret of) strength.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest; that which has no (substantial) existence enters where there is no crevice.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: It is because he is thus free from striving that therefore no one in the world is able to strive with him.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: Man takes his law from the Earth; the Earth takes its law from Heaven; Heaven takes its law from the Tao.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike.
quotes.author: Lao Tzu

quotes.text: Simulated disorder postulates perfect discipline; simulated fear postulates courage; simulated weakness postulates strength.
quotes.author: Sun Tzu

quotes.text: Anger may in time change to gladness; vexation may be succeeded by content.
quotes.author: Sun Tzu

quotes.text: All men can see the tactics whereby I conquer, but what none can see is the strategy out of which victory is evolved.
quotes.author: Sun Tzu

quotes.text: The difficulty of tactical manœuvering consists in turning the devious into the direct, and misfortune into gain.
quotes.author: Sun Tzu

quotes.text: Wherefore, O judges, be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: Above all, I shall then be able to continue my search into true and false knowledge; as in this world, so also in the next; and I shall find out who is wise, and who pretends to be wise, and is not.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue comes money and every other good of man, public as well as private.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death, but to avoid unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: Never mind the manner, which may or may not be good; but think only of the truth of my words, and give heed to that: let the speaker speak truly and the judge decide justly.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: I thought at the time that I ought not to do anything common or mean when in danger: nor do I now repent of the style of my defence; I would rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: In another world they do not put a man to death for asking questions: assuredly not.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: The hour of departure has arrived, and we go our ways—I to die, and you to live.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: The man who compares grey with black, calls grey white; and the man who compares absence of pain with pain, calls the absence of pain pleasure.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: Hope,’ he says, ‘cherishes the soul of him who lives in justice and holiness, and is the nurse of his age and the companion of his journey;—hope which is mightiest to sway the restless soul of man.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser—God is justified.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: A wise man whispers to me that the pleasures of the wise are true and pure; all others are a shadow only.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: The true lover of learning then must from his earliest youth, as far as in him lies, desire all truth?
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: All things end in good to him, either in life or after death, even what appears to be evil; for the Gods have a care of him who desires to be in their likeness.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: A man of sense ought not to say, nor will I be very confident, that the description which I have given of the soul and her mansions is exactly true.
quotes.author: Plato

quotes.text: The multitude of men seem to be deceived by reason of pleasure, because though it is not really a good it impresses their minds with the notion of goodness, so they choose what is pleasant as good and avoid pain as an evil.
quotes.author: Aristotle

quotes.text: Furthermore, the good man wishes to continue to live with himself; for he can do it with pleasure, in that his memories of past actions are full of delight and his anticipations of the future are good and such are pleasurable.
quotes.author: Aristotle

quotes.text: Virtue, must be a state whereby Man comes to be good and whereby he will perform well his proper work.
quotes.author: Aristotle

quotes.text: The man therefore who is to come up to our notion “Happy” will need good Friends.
quotes.author: Aristotle

quotes.text: We are right then in saying, that these virtues are formed in a man by his doing the actions; but no one, if he should leave them undone, would be even in the way to become a good man.
quotes.author: Aristotle

quotes.text: On the other hand, it looks absurd, while we are assigning to the Happy man all other good things, not to give him Friends, which are, after all, thought to be the greatest of external goods.
quotes.author: Aristotle

quotes.text: If then to be thus is exceedingly wretched it is a man’s duty to flee from wickedness with all his might and to strive to be good, because thus may he be friends with himself and may come to be a friend to another.
quotes.author: Aristotle

quotes.text: Let this, then, be laid down as the first law of friendship, that we should ask from friends, and do for friends', only what is good.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: To begin with, how can life be worth living, to use the words of Ennius, which lacks that repose which is to be found in the mutual good-will of a friend?
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: The true rule is to take such care in the selection of our friends as never to enter upon a friendship with a man whom we could under any circumstances come to hate.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: A gloomy temper and unvarying gravity may be very impressive; but friendship should be a little less unbending, more indulgent and gracious, and more inclined to all kinds of good-fellowship and good-nature.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: Accordingly, the death of young men seems to me like putting out a great fire with a deluge of water; but old men die like a fire going out because it has burnt down of its own nature without artificial means.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: Virtue (without which friendship is impossible) is first; but next to it, and to it alone, the greatest of all things is Friendship.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: Men, of course, who have no resources in themselves for securing a good and happy life find every age burdensome.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: Hours indeed, and days and months and years depart, nor does past time ever return, nor can the future be known.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: The great affairs of life are not performed by physical strength, or activity, or nimbleness of body, but by deliberation, character, expression of opinion.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: If, however, the truth rather is that the body and soul perish together, and that no sensation remains, then though there is nothing good in death, at least there is nothing bad.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: Whatever time each is granted for life, with that he is bound to be content.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: In the face of a true friend a man sees as it were a second self.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: All I can do is to urge on you to regard friendship as the greatest thing in the world; for there is nothing which so fits in with our nature, or is so exactly what we want in prosperity or adversity.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: We must look after our health, use moderate exercise, take just enough food and drink to recruit, but not to overload, our strength.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: You might just as well take the sun out of the sky as friendship from life; for the immortal gods have given us nothing better or more delightful.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: Let there be only a proper husbanding of strength, and let each man proportion his efforts to his powers.
quotes.author: Cicero
quotes.work: On Friendship and On Old Age

quotes.text: The real limit to be observed in friendship is this: the characters of two friends must be stainless.
quotes.author: Cicero

quotes.text: Few things are needed to make a wise man happy; nothing can make a fool content; that is why most men are miserable.
quotes.author: La Rochefoucauld

quotes.text: Self-love is the love of self, and of all things for self.
quotes.author: La Rochefoucauld

quotes.text: We imitate good actions by emulation, and bad ones by the evil of our nature, which shame imprisons until example liberates.
quotes.author: La Rochefoucauld

quotes.text: The greedy man is nearly always desirous to possess, and often foregoes great future advantages for small present interests.
quotes.author: La Rochefoucauld

quotes.text: We should make our pleasure that of other persons, to humour, never to wound their self-love.
quotes.author: La Rochefoucauld

quotes.text: We should readily excuse our friends when their faults are born with them, and they are less than their good qualities.
quotes.author: La Rochefoucauld

quotes.text: We often imitate the same person without perceiving it, and we neglect our own good qualities for the good qualities of others, which generally do not suit us.
quotes.author: La Rochefoucauld

quotes.text: The labour of the body frees us from the pains of the mind, and thus makes the poor happy.
quotes.author: La Rochefoucauld

quotes.text: The mind's highest good is the knowledge of God, and the mind's highest virtue is to know God.
quotes.author: Baruch Spinoza

quotes.text: The good which every man, who follows after virtue, desires for himself he will also desire for other men, and so much the more, in proportion as he has a greater knowledge of God.
quotes.author: Baruch Spinoza

quotes.text: A free man thinks of death least of all things; and his wisdom is a meditation not of death but of life.
quotes.author: Baruch Spinoza

quotes.text: A man is as much affected pleasurably or painfully by the image of a thing past or future as by the image of a thing present.
quotes.author: Baruch Spinoza

quotes.text: If men were born free, they would, so long as they remained free, form no conception of good and evil.
quotes.author: Baruch Spinoza

quotes.text: By highmindedness I mean the desire whereby every man endeavours, solely under the dictates of reason, to aid other men and to unite them to himself in friendship.
quotes.author: Baruch Spinoza

quotes.text: The reason or cause why God or Nature exists, and the reason why he acts, are one and the same.
quotes.author: Baruch Spinoza

quotes.text: He, who lives under the guidance of reason, endeavours, as far as possible, to render back love, or kindness, for other men's hatred, anger, contempt, &c., towards him.
quotes.author: Baruch Spinoza

quotes.text: Leisure, is Time for doing something useful; this Leisure the diligent Man will obtain, but the lazy Man never; so that, as Poor Richard says, A Life of Leisure and a Life of Laziness are two things.
quotes.author: Benjamin Franklin

quotes.text: When I saw one too ambitious of court favor, sacrificing his time in attendance on levees, his repose, his liberty, his virtue, and perhaps his friends, to attain it, I have said to myself, This man gives too much for his whistle.
quotes.author: Benjamin Franklin

quotes.text: As I grew up, came into the world, and observed the actions of men, I thought I met with many, very many, who gave too much for the whistle.
quotes.author: Benjamin Franklin

quotes.text: Beware of little expenses; A small Leak will sink a great Ship; and again, Who Dainties love, shall Beggars prove; and moreover, Fools make Feasts, and wise Men eat them.
quotes.author: Benjamin Franklin

quotes.text: I will tell thee, my friend, what Poor Richard says, Employ thy Time well, if thou meanest to gain Leisure; and, since thou art not sure of a Minute, throw not away an Hour.
quotes.author: Benjamin Franklin

quotes.text: A wise man will extend this lesson to all parts of life, and know that it is the part of prudence to face every claimant and pay every just demand on your time, your talents, or your heart.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: A mind might ponder its thought for ages and not gain so much self-knowledge as the passion of love shall teach it in a day.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: Every revolution was first a thought in one man’s mind, and when the same thought occurs to another man, it is the key to that era.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: To believe your own thought, to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men,—that is genius.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: One man’s justice is another’s injustice; one man’s beauty another’s ugliness; one man’s wisdom another’s folly; as one beholds the same objects from a higher point.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: Whenever a mind is simple and receives a divine wisdom, old things pass away,—means, teachers, texts, temples fall; it lives now, and absorbs past and future into the present hour.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: Man is the broken giant, and in all his weakness both his body and his mind are invigorated by habits of conversation with nature.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: We judge of a man’s wisdom by his hope, knowing that the perception of the inexhaustibleness of nature is an immortal youth.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: Men imagine that they communicate their virtue or vice only by overt actions, and do not see that virtue or vice emit a breath every moment.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: A thrill passes through all men at the reception of new truth, or at the performance of a great action, which comes out of the heart of nature.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: A man is relieved and gay when he has put his heart into his work and done his best; but what he has said or done otherwise shall give him no peace.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: To truth, justice, love, the attributes of the soul, the idea of immutableness is essentially associated.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: He cannot be happy and strong until he too lives with nature in the present, above time.
quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

quotes.text: To be a philosopher is not merely to have subtle thoughts, nor even to found a school, but so to love wisdom as to live according to its dictates, a life of simplicity, independence, magnanimity, and trust.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: I came into this world, not chiefly to make this a good place to live in, but to live in it, be it good or bad.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: Every morning was a cheerful invitation to make my life of equal simplicity, and I may say innocence, with Nature herself.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: The gentle rain which waters my beans and keeps me in the house to-day is not drear and melancholy, but good for me too.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: The best thing a man can do for his culture when he is rich is to endeavor to carry out those schemes which he entertained when he was poor.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: Men esteem truth remote, in the outskirts of the system, behind the farthest star, before Adam and after the last man.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: If I were confined to a corner of a garret all my days, like a spider, the world would be just as large to me while I had my thoughts about me.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: The greater part of what my neighbors call good I believe in my soul to be bad, and if I repent of anything, it is very likely to be my good behavior.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: Men say that a stitch in time saves nine, and so they take a thousand stitches to-day to save nine to-morrow.
quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau

quotes.text: A good, temperate, gentle character can be happy in needy circumstances, whilst a covetous, envious and malicious man, even if he be the richest in the world, goes miserable.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: The man to whom nature and fate have granted the blessing of wisdom, will be most anxious and careful to keep open the fountains of happiness which he has in himself; and for this, independence and leisure are necessary.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: The world in which a man lives shapes itself chiefly by the way in which he looks at it, and so it proves different to different men; to one it is barren, dull, and superficial; to another rich, interesting, and full of meaning.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: The man who is cheerful and merry has always a good reason for being so,—the fact, namely, that he is so.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: In such a world as this, a man who is rich in himself is like a bright, warm, happy room at Christmastide, while without are the frost and snow of a December night.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: The influence of an action, be it never so noble, can last but a short time; but a work of genius is a living influence, beneficial and ennobling throughout the ages.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: Life is such a poor business that the strictest economy must be exercised in its good things.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: Only under a favorable fate like this can a man be said to be born free, to be, in the proper sense of the word, sui juris, master of his own time and powers, and able to say every morning, This day is my own.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: A man never feels the loss of things which it never occurs to him to ask for; he is just as happy without them; whilst another, who may have a hundred times as much, feels miserable because he has not got the one thing he wants.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: We have already seen, in general, that what a man is contributes much more to his happiness than what he has, or how he is regarded by others.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: A man can be himself only so long as he is alone; and if he does not love solitude, he will not love freedom; for it is only when he is alone that he is really free.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: Peace of mind! that is something essential to any enjoyment of the present moment; and unless its separate moments are enjoyed, there is an end of life's happiness as a whole.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: A man who is always preparing for either class of evil will not have a moment of peace left him.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: The present alone is true and actual; it is the only time which possesses full reality, and our existence lies in it exclusively.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: We are happy in proportion as our range of vision, our sphere of work, our points of contact with the world, are restricted and circumscribed.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: The young should early be trained to bear being left alone; for it is a source of happiness and peace of mind.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: He who can see truly in the midst of general infatuation is like a man whose watch keeps good time, when all clocks in the town in which he lives are wrong.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: A man shows his character just in the way in which he deals with trifles,—for then he is off his guard.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: Instead of finding, as we expected, pleasure, happiness, joy, we get experience, insight, knowledge—a real and permanent blessing, instead of a fleeting and illusory one.
quotes.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

quotes.text: Men of profound sadness betray themselves when they are happy: they have a mode of seizing upon happiness as though they would choke and strangle it, out of jealousy—ah, they know only too well that it will flee from them!
quotes.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

quotes.text: The greatest events and thoughts—the greatest thoughts, however, are the greatest events—are longest in being comprehended: the generations which are contemporary with them do not EXPERIENCE such events—they live past them.
quotes.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

quotes.text: A man's estimates of value betray something of the STRUCTURE of his soul, and wherein it sees its conditions of life, its intrinsic needs.
quotes.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

quotes.text: Whoever has seen deeply into the world has doubtless divined what wisdom there is in the fact that men are superficial.
quotes.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

quotes.text: The discipline of suffering, of GREAT suffering—know ye not that it is only THIS discipline that has produced all the elevations of humanity hitherto?
quotes.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

quotes.text: The belly is the reason why man does not so readily take himself for a God.
quotes.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

quotes.text: The distance, and as it were the space around man, grows with the strength of his intellectual vision and insight: his world becomes profounder; new stars, new enigmas, and notions are ever coming into view.
quotes.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
